newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia/MidEast condensate output to triple -- study.
newsitem.headline: Asia/MidEast condensate output to triple -- study.

text.p: Condensate production in the Mid-east and Asia-Pacific region is set to triple to 3 million barrels-per-day (bpd) by 2010 but new markets need to be found for the additional output as more than half is currently put back into the crude oil pool, a study said.

One new market which may give producers' steady returns is power generation, a joint-study by Hawaii-based Fesharaki Associates Consulting & Technical Services (FACT) and Malaysia-based Asia Pacific Energy Consulting (APEC) said.

"Although the power market for condensates is still largely speculative (and maybe banned in some countries), most condensates makes an outstanding gas-turbine feed," the group said in a press statement marking the study, "Condensate Outlook East of Suez Through 2010".
"Its low sulphur, metals and salt content simultaneously protect turbines and other parts while keeping pollution low."
Alternatively, it said producers could get together with consumers to jointly build condensate projects which would guarantee price stability to the buyer and a captive market to the seller.

Condensates are hydrocarbon gases that are heavier than liquified petroleum gas (LPG) but lighter than crude oil and are rich in naphtha, diesel and jet fuel but the extraction of these lucrative petroleum products are expensive.

For now, just under half of condensates produced hit the export market directly, with about 20 percent used in domestic refining in producing countries and about 18 percent spiked back into the domestic crude oil pool.
Many produers also have field seperation units so as to end up with only a naphtha-range cut such as the Saudi Master Gas System.
As a result, Saudi condensate ends up as Saudi A-180 naphtha, a premium feed for petrochemical producers.
Producing countries are usually in the fore front in undertaking projects that either consume or process the condensates via splitter units to yield petroleum products.
The study said two splitters are being built in Abu Dhabi each capable of producing 140,000-bpd of products.
"Splitters use the same tehcnology and materials as refinery distillation towers and can be built to the same scale," the report said.

Condensate use among Asian endusers is limited because they are difficult to refine, cost a lot of money to transport, and petrochemical plants are not equipped to process them in large volumes, the study said.
"Running condensates instead of crude can cut the effective capacity of a typical distillation column in half and produce more material than can be handled by downstream processing units," it said.

The report also said that even if petrochemical producers are willing to use the condensates they would not be willing to pay the premium condensates command because of its high middle-distillate content.
